I will keep my farm management conservative and practical. I am 65, I have 40 years of farming experience, and my land is only 10.1 mu, so I will not chase risky changes. Because my farm already follows a wheat-maize system and I have well irrigation, I will keep most of the land in that rotation for stable grain output and cash flow, and I will keep a smaller piece in cotton because I already know how to manage it and it spreads my risk. Some family members work off-farm, so I will also choose practices that fit limited labor: improved or hybrid seed where it clearly helps, moderate fertilizer instead of very high rates, rotary tillage because it is easier for me to manage, and a limited number of irrigations and sprays based on the crops’ main needs.

For wheat, I will put it on 7.0 mu through the winter season, then follow that same land with summer maize. I will use improved wheat seed because I want better stand and steadier yield without making management too complicated. I will apply enough nitrogen to support tillering and grain filling, with phosphorus for rooting and some potassium for plant strength. Since I have well irrigation, I will irrigate at the key times rather than too often. For maize on the same 7.0 mu, I will use hybrid seed because maize responds well and gives me the best return on that land after wheat. I will feed maize with more nitrogen than wheat, give enough phosphorus and potassium, and irrigate a few times if rainfall is not enough. For cotton, I will keep 3.1 mu. I will use improved seed, not something too fancy, because I want dependable performance and manageable cost. Cotton needs more crop protection work than wheat and maize, so I will plan more pesticide applications there and keep fertilizer moderate so the crop does not grow too vegetatively. This is the kind of plan I would actually use myself: stable, familiar, and suitable for my age, labor situation, and irrigated conditions.
